beats.say: JCPenney stopped coupons. And prices stayed the same.
Every item shows a single "Fair and Square" price, no sales tags.
The same price appears on all merchandise, from jeans to appliances.
No extra discounts, just one flat price per product.
Sales fell 25% and the company lost $985 million. Looks disastrous.
But the new list was a decoy, not a discount.
Shoppers chase the feeling of a discount, not the actual low price.
The everyday-price option made every tag look like a deal, so the cheap baseline vanished.
Without a clear lower price, customers spent less, driving the 25% sales drop and $985 million loss.
You see it everywhere. A coffee shop lists a plain brew, a flavored latte, and a premium pour-over.
The latte costs $2.50, the plain brew $2, the pour-over $4.
The mid-priced latte feels like the smart choice, nudging people away from the cheap option.
If a price list removes the obvious discount, assume it's a trick. Follow for more.
